name: Dancer
description: Dancer by Helene Brox catches a cream figure mid-stride on a sky blue ground, arms rippling like ribbons caught in their own momentum. There is no face and no floor, just the shape of movement itself, one arm curling back while the other reaches high, painted with the loose confidence of a paper cut-out. It reads clearly from right across a room, and it brings genuine motion to a calm one.

name: Dragon
description: Dragon by Helene Brox coils across a black ground in ribbons of white, red, pink and grey, a beast glimpsed in fragments rather than drawn whole. Find the pale blue eyes and the composition snaps into focus; relax, and it dissolves back into pure rhythm. The most energetic piece in Brox's collection sits closer to pattern than portrait, and the black ground gives every colour real bite. One for a wall that can hold its nerve.

name: Eltsjoen
description: Eltsjoen by Ingunn Dybendal reimagines a Nordic lake landscape as dense coloured-pencil pattern: pink sky, dark mountain, patterned forest, blue water. Every band of the scene becomes ornament: clouds stretched into ribbons, trees turned to folk motifs, the water pooling in pale rings around a bridge. It is the most detailed piece in the gallery, drawn stroke by stroke, and it rewards the hundredth look as much as the first.

name: Eye Nose Eye
description: Eye Nose Eye by Simen Wahlqvist turns a face into a Venn diagram: two overlapping circles labelled eye and eye, and where they meet, nose. A bald cream head on a near-black ground wears the diagram as spectacles, yellow and red circles meeting in blue. Wahlqvist works in as few lines as possible and reckons a drawing is done when it makes him laugh; this one clearly qualified. Dry, tidy and quietly ridiculous.

name: Half Man
description: Half Man by Simen Wahlqvist splits a pink figure clean in two on a bright green ground, the torso arching over backwards while the legs stand firm. The head hovers in the gap between the halves, wearing an expression somewhere between effort and mild complaint. It is drawn with Wahlqvist's usual economy, a handful of lines and two colours doing all the work, and it makes an absurd, deadpan anchor for a hallway or desk wall.

name: Hummer og Vin
description: Hummer og Vin by Sia Siamos looks straight down on a summer table: a whole lobster on a blue platter, lemons, vine tomatoes and glasses of red wine. Hands reach in from the edges, candles lean at friendly angles, and grapes and carrots crowd the green cloth, all painted loose enough that the scene feels mid-conversation. The title is Norwegian for lobster and wine, and the print keeps exactly that promise: a long, generous evening, held mid-toast.

name: Hyttefrokost
description: Hyttefrokost by Sia Siamos piles ripe tomatoes, grapes and a carafe of water against green kitchen tiles, drawn in bold, joyful colour. The title means cabin breakfast in Norwegian, and the drawing has that holiday ease: big tomatoes heaped on a striped board, cherry tomatoes scattering across a lilac table, a yellow checked cloth thrown down rather than laid. Every outline is quick and confident, closer to a sketchbook page than a formal still life.

name: IThinkIThink
description: IThinkIThink by Helene Brox spells out its confession, I think I think too much, in green brush strokes across a cobalt head on shocking pink. Red squiggles loop through the profile like thoughts refusing to settle, and two wide, mismatched eyes complete the picture of a brain at full volume. The loudest print in the gallery, and the most instantly likeable; buy it for the person whose mind never sits down, even if that person is you.

name: Mean Snothing
description: Mean Snothing by Simen Wahlqvist gives an orange man a Newton's cradle for eyes, one ball caught mid-swing, on a flat green ground. The face underneath stays perfectly deadpan, which is the whole joke: physics happening on a forehead and nobody reacting. Drawn in Wahlqvist's spare, confident line, it is the kind of print that gets a second look from every guest, and it earns its place in a home office better than any motivational poster.

name: Morgenlevering
description: Morgenlevering by Sia Siamos paints a breakfast table in full swing: cafetière coffee, croissants on a checked cloth, pink carnations in a red vase. Morning light falls through the window onto a warm terracotta table crowded with cups, sliced bread and a water carafe, everything tilted towards you as if you have just pulled up a chair. The name translates as morning delivery, which is about right: the whole table feels newly arrived.

name: Morgenstrekk
description: Morgenstrekk by Simen Wahlqvist catches the day's first full-body stretch, a figure reaching for a small sun with a charging cable wound around him. The cable trails down to a plug at the skirting board, as though he has just unplugged himself from the night and is charging off the morning instead. Ochre on warm peach, drawn in Wahlqvist's handful of lines, it is the gentlest and most optimistic of his prints.

name: Slingshot
description: Slingshot by Simen Wahlqvist strings elastic between two raised fingers and loads a small, contented figure into the palm below, ready to fly. A peace sign turned catapult, drawn in white on a bright tomato red ground with the fewest lines the joke will allow. The figure looks entirely relaxed about what happens next, which is somehow the funniest part. A square print with a proper glint in its eye.

name: Swallow Dive
description: Swallow Dive by Helene Brox fills the frame edge to edge with diving birds in deep cobalt, bold cut-out shapes swooping over warm cream. There is no horizon and no resting point, just the repeated plunge of wings that turns a flock into pattern. The two-colour discipline is what makes it: one blue, one cream, and all the movement carried by shape alone. Calm enough for a bedroom, confident enough for the room where guests land.

name: Tree Top Peach
description: Tree Top Peach by Helene Brox weaves branches and perched birds into a soft peach lattice, papercut style, inside its own drawn border. Look longer and the birds keep arriving: dozens of small silhouettes tucked among the tangle, all in a single warm tone on cream. It is the gentlest print in the gallery, closer to folk papercut than illustration, and it settles a bedroom or reading corner without disappearing into it.

name: Trysilkaffe
description: Trysilkaffe by Ingunn Dybendal crams a green mug with an impossible bouquet, folk flowers in red, purple and teal above a diamond-check cloth. Every bloom is a different invention, daisies, rosettes and seed heads drawn petal by petal in coloured pencil, and even the mug carries its own tulip motif. It is pattern on pattern on pattern, cheerfully too much in the best Nordic folk tradition, and it wakes up any wall it hangs on.

name: Vinkveld
description: Vinkveld by Sia Siamos paints a wine evening in thick, glossy strokes: a glass of red, green olives, dark grapes and vine tomatoes against checked tiles. A bottle stands in the foreground with the cork already adrift, which tells you where the evening is heading. Vinkveld means wine evening, and the brushwork agrees, thicker and moodier than Siamos's other table scenes, with the checked tiles dissolving into loose strokes behind. One for a kitchen or dining wall.
